primary_new_grammar.label: Passato remoto (3rd person) in narration against the present in dialogue; articles and articulated prepositions; gender and number; essere/avere; c'è/ci sono; tu/voi address

cover.alt: A Florentine street at Porta San Piero in 1299: a shearer and his son stop at the door of a merchant shop.
cover.art_brief: Florence, a cool October morning in 1299, a street in the sesto of Porta San Piero near the Cerchi houses: tall stone house-towers, a shop front open to the street under a wooden awning, bales of wool visible inside and a long counter in shadow. At the threshold stand Cione, a tired cloth-shearer about 45 in a worn tunic and apron, and his son Lapo, sixteen, lean and dark-haired, in his best plain tunic. Cione stays outside the doorway; Lapo looks in. Ink outline and restrained watercolour wash. No text, lettering, numbers or captions anywhere.

inference_aids.alt: Ser Bindo weighs a florin at the counter while the Donati man waits and Lapo watches.
inference_aids.art_brief: At this segment: late morning, October 1299, the Cerchi company shop near the Cerchi houses at Porta San Piero, Florence. Daylight from the open street door. A long wooden counter with a large open account book and a small balance for coin. Ser Bindo, an old thin clean-shaven bookkeeper in a dark long gown and close cap, holds a small gold florin over the pan of the balance and looks at it, not at the customer. Across the counter stands the Donati man, a big man about 35 in a short belted tunic and hood, one hand flat on a folded length of cloth that lies on the counter. Behind the counter, a little apart, Lapo, a lean dark-haired boy of sixteen in a plain tunic, empty-handed, watches Bindo. Two young clerks in the background have stopped counting cloth. Bales of wool and folded cloth on shelves. No weapons drawn. Ink outline and restrained watercolour wash. No text, lettering, numbers or captions anywhere.

words_with_history.title: Dal latino all'italiano
words_with_history.text: Ser Bindo disse tre numeri. Lapo fece il conto, e vide la somma. Lapo entrò nella bottega, e la bottega fu la sua casa.
words_with_history.note_en:
The passato remoto continues the Latin perfect, often with the same strong stem: fuit → fu, habuit → ebbe, dixit → disse, fecit → fece, vidit → vide, venit → venne. Regular -are verbs continue the perfect in -avit: intravit → entrò, with the stress kept on the ending (hence the written accent). Treat these as correspondences to recognise, not a cipher: mise continues misit, but prese and rispose follow the s-pattern of disse and mise, which Latin prehendit and respondit did not have.

The article grew out of ille: illum → il (and lo), illam → la. Latin had no word for "the"; Italian uses il and la to mark a thing as known or specific (il libro: the book on Bindo's counter), against un libro, any book.

Nouns usually continue the Latin accusative and lose its final -m: librum → libro, portam → porta, errorem → errore, partem → parte; civitatem → città.

One Latin verb gave two Italian ones: pensare "weigh, ponder" became pesare "weigh" (Bindo weighs the florin) and pensare "think" (Lapo thinks of his father).

Words whose Latin source meant something else: casa is Latin casa "hut", but in Italian it is the ordinary house and home (domus); cosa "thing" is Latin causa; mettere "put" is Latin mittere "send"; giorno "day" is diurnum "of the day".

grammar.note_en:
**Narration in the passato remoto, speech in the present.** The narration moves forward in the passato remoto, the Italian descendant of the Latin perfect: disse (dixit), vide (vidit), fece (fecit), venne (venit), fu (fuit), ebbe (habuit). What people say is in the present: «Io non entro» (I'm not going in), «Quanto fa?» (What does it make?). Bindo's test shows the split: he asks in the present, and the narrator reports in the remoto: Lapo fece il conto una volta, poi un'altra (Lapo did the sum once, then again). When Lapo tells Gherardo about his day he uses the present too: «Oggi entro nella bottega, e Ser Bindo fa un errore» (Today I walk into the shop, and Ser Bindo makes a mistake), as English does in a lively story. The present can also refer to the future, as in English: «Fra dieci anni io sono a Roma» (In ten years I'll be in Rome); «Domani vieni prima del sole» (Tomorrow come before sunrise). Spoken Italian also has a compound past, ha fatto (has done), from chapter 4 on. In the table Disse e dice, the left column is the passato remoto and the right the present. The remoto is the tense of written narrative from Dante and the chroniclers to modern novels.

**Forms.** For now you need the third person. The regular -are verbs of this chapter end in -ò in the singular and -arono in the plural: entra → entrò, guarda → guardò (looked), pesa → pesò (weighed), conta → contò (counted); contarono, guardarono (they counted, they looked). The written accent on -ò marks the stress. Andare (andò, went) and stare (stette, stood) are irregular. Many common verbs have strong forms, as in Latin, and are learned as words: disse (said), vide (saw), fece (did), venne (came), mise (put), prese (took), rispose (answered), fu (was), ebbe (had). Learn the plurals as pairs: disse/dissero, vide/videro, stette/stettero. For description in the past the narrator uses era (was) and c'era (there was): Al banco un vecchio pesò l'oro, but Era la bottega della compagnia di messer Vieri (It was the shop of messer Vieri's company). Era is an imperfect, the tense of chapter 3.

**Articles.** Latin had none; Italian made them from ille. Masculine il (il banco), l' before a vowel (l'oro, l'uomo), plural i (i panni), and gli before s + consonant or a vowel (gli Spini); feminine la (la porta), l' before a vowel, plural le (le case). Indefinite: un (un fiorino), una (una somma), un' before a vowel in the feminine (un'altra volta). The masculine lo and uno, used before s + consonant and z, come later.

**Prepositions with the article.** Di, a, da, in and su join the article that follows: su + il = sul (sul banco, on the counter), in + la = nella (nella bottega, in the shop), di + i = dei (dei Cerchi, of the Cerchi), di + gli = degli (amici degli Spini, friends of the Spini), da + gli = dagli (Dagli Spini, at the Spini's). Da with a person or a family means "at the house or shop of", like French chez: dagli Spini, at the Spini bank. Di + article can also mean "some": dell'oro (some gold) beside dei Cerchi (of the Cerchi). De' is the older short form of dei, still usual in names: Vieri de' Cerchi.

**Gender and number.** Nouns and adjectives agree, as in Latin, with fewer endings: masculine -o, plural -i (il ragazzo nuovo, the new boy; nuovi ricchi, new rich men); feminine -a, plural -e (la casa, le case: the house, the houses); -e, plural -i, for either gender (il mercante, i mercanti: the merchant, the merchants; un grande libro, a big book). Città does not change in the plural. Possessives usually take the article (i tuoi padroni, your masters; i loro panni, their cloths), but not before a singular word for a relative: suo padre (his father), suo marito (her husband), sua sorella (his sister).

**Essere, avere; c'è, ci sono.** The present: io sono, tu sei, è, voi siete, sono (Io sono un cimatore; I Cerchi sono ricchi); tu hai, ha, hanno. C'è means "there is" and ci sono "there are": «Sul fiorino c'è San Giovanni» (On the florin there is St John); «Dagli Spini ci sono mille fiorini» (At the Spini's there are a thousand florins). Mi chiamo Lapo (My name is Lapo) is literally "I call myself Lapo".

**Tu and voi.** Bindo says tu to Lapo (Quanti anni hai? How old are you?); Lapo says voi to Bindo and calls him messere (Vedete, messere: You see, sir). Tu is for equals, family and juniors; voi is respect, to an elder, a master or a customer: Bindo gives voi to the Donati man (Il fiorino è vostro: The florin is yours). Modern standard Italian uses Lei, a third-person form, for formal address; it spread from the sixteenth century, and nobody in this story uses it. Dante writes voi.

**Older forms.** A few older forms appear, each glossed in the margin at first use: de' (dei), messere or messer (sir, title of knights and judges), Ser (title of a notary), Monna (title of a married woman), ché (perché, because), niuno (nessuno, nobody). Older people use them more than the young.

C.title: C
C.instruction: Questions 1–2: answer in Italian or English, in your own words, then compare with the model. Questions 3–4 are Dal latino all'italiano, in English or Italian. (3) Write the Italian passato remoto from the story for each Latin perfect, in this order: fuit, habuit, fecit, venit, intravit. (4) Latin says Lapus lanam et pannos vidit. What do la and i add that the Latin has no word for?

items.prompt: Ser Bindo mise cinquantadue nel libro. Che cosa fece Lapo?
model_answers: Lapo fece il conto e disse: «Messere, non fa cinquantadue. Fa quarantotto.»
items.rubric: Lapo does the sum twice and corrects the old man's figure instead of agreeing with it, politely (messere, voi), and holds to it when Bindo points to the book. Bindo then writes forty-eight and hires him («Domani vieni prima del sole»). An English answer is fine.

items.prompt: Perché Ser Bindo mise cinquantadue nel libro?
model_answers: Per vedere se Lapo dice: «Sì, messere», o se dice: «La somma è quarantotto».
items.rubric: It was a test, and the error was deliberate: Bindo wanted to see whether the boy would agree with a wrong figure to please him or contradict him. After the Donati man leaves, Bindo says the man came «per vedere se i Cerchi prendono oro scarso», and adds «Come io con te, ragazzo»: a sum that does not add up is like a coin short of weight. An English answer is fine.

fuit → fu (Gherardo fu con Lapo all'abaco); habuit → ebbe (Lapo ebbe un padrone); fecit → fece (Lapo fece il conto); venit → venne (venne alla bottega un uomo grande); intravit → entrò (Lapo entrò). All are third person singular, as the Latin is.

items.prompt: Lapo vide la lana e i panni.
model_answers: «La lana» e «i panni»: quella lana e quei panni, nella bottega dei Cerchi.
items.rubric: They are definite articles: "the wool and the cloths". La (feminine singular) and i (masculine plural) mark lana and panni as particular, known things, the wool and cloth in that shop, where Latin leaves this to context. The forms come from Latin ille: illam → la, illum → il.

provenance.author: Claude Opus 5.5
notes: Model chapter 1 of design v4, written by Claude Opus 5.5 from plan/cards/ch01.md for the owner's reading. Draft; no audio; pictures planned only, none generated.

Story choices inside the card's beats: Bindo enters the wrong sum in the big book (mise ... nel libro) rather than on a wax tablet, so contradicting him means contradicting the book (seed for 'il libro non torna'); Lapo therefore holds nothing in the planned counting-room picture, and its art brief says so. After the Donati man leaves, Bindo admits the error was a test («Come io con te, ragazzo»), tying the false sum to the light coin. Lapo keeps that from Gherardo («Lapo non disse tutto»). Card scene 3 says the Donati man leaves 'with his cloth unpaid-for'; here Bindo keeps the cloth and hands back the florin («Il fiorino è vostro, e il panno sta qui»), which follows the plan row's 'refuses it courteously' and makes the humiliation public. The ch10 payoff (the man remembers Bindo) works either way; the card wording should be reconciled by the owner.

Sums are in florins only: soldo, pagare, scrivere, potere, volere, tavola and the forms fanno, dicono, sapete are planned for chapter 2, so the text writes around them (the Donati man 'mise sul banco un fiorino').

Incidentals glossed at first use and then declared in learning_contract.incidental: anni (anno is a chapter 2 lexeme), prima (function word from chapter 2), papa (chapter 2 lexeme). Selvaggi, villani, arricchiti, abaco and parte are single glossed uses, not lexemes.

All are real Latin with the sense used. Banco is glossed tabula as a same-sense word, not an etymon (banco is Germanic).

Lexemes: 64 new, within the ceiling of 75: the 62 planned items in use plus pensare and volta. Planned cavallo, piccolo and male are dropped (no natural use; propose moving them to chapter 2 or later). The chapter 8 model writer's delta also declares pensare, volta and some chapter 1 forms (entri); chapter 1 forms carry first_lesson it-dante-01-l01 explicitly so the merge keeps them here.

Recurrence: after review, cosa, chiamare, lavorare, città, mercante, numero, somma, sorella and marito were brought to three uses by recombination inside existing beats. Seven planned lexemes stay below three (ricco 2, falso 2, sole 2, Monna 2, povero 1, giorno 1, sera 1), and five glossed single uses (selvaggi, villani, arricchiti, all'abaco, parte) are not lexemes. RULES §4 requires three uses and COURSE.md's only exception covers quotations, so this is NOT an authorized waiver: it is put to the owner as a design question (review question RQ-recurrence). Raising them further would need padding.

The Dal latino all'italiano exercise is the second block of Pensa C: the lesson schema allows only A, B and C, and section exercises would go to a workbook, which this course does not have. Pensa C therefore has four items (two story questions, two Latin), and the chapter has ten items in all: A4, B2, C2 + Latino 2.

Primary target: passato remoto in narration against the present in dialogue, shown from the first line («Io non entro», disse Cione) and dozens of times; strong forms disse, vide, fece, venne, fu, ebbe, mise, prese, rispose, stette; regular -ò/-arono. Narration uses era/c'era for description (receptive in G01).

Register level 1 only: de', messer(e), Ser, Monna, ché, niuno, each glossed with its standard twin or sense at first use. Older speakers carry them (Cione: ché; the Donati man: niuno; Bindo and Lapo: messere).

History follows the card: the Cerchi of Acone, Calimala merchant-bankers, at Porta San Piero next to the Donati; the Spini bankers to Boniface VIII; the florin with St John; Corso Donati is not mentioned (banished in May 1299). The company shop and all named commoners are fictional. No exchange rate is stated.
Word count 945 against a 1,100 target (window 900–1,300, advisory): five scenes, each with a want and a turn; not padded.

Independent Codex review (cx job 1108-124753-24713, GPT-6.1-Sol, high): linguistic and pedagogical verdicts 'blocked' on seven points, all addressed: Agli Spini → Dagli Spini (with da + family = chez in the note and table); false claims in the Forms paragraph rewritten (andare, stare irregular; strong plurals learned as pairs; fu's plural not stated); C02–C04 model answers now answer their tasks; banco glossed at its first occurrence; all'abaco glossed schola abaci (replacing abacus, which does not give the school sense); messer and Monna glossed with their standard twins signore and signora (Latin dominus/domina moved to the English reveal); recurrence raised and the remainder put to the owner. Suggestions taken: partitive dell'oro, possessives without article before kin, present for future, translations of table examples, messere vocative to the retainer removed (voi kept), continuity log qualified.
